content: Cholera is an acute diarrheal illness characterized by profuse watery diarrhea, which can lead to severe dehydration and death if not promptly and adequately treated. It typically occurs in epidemic settings and is strongly associated with conditions of poverty and inadequate sanitation. The development and use of effective, affordable, and easy-to-administer vaccines could play a critical role in preventing cholera outbreaks. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of oral cholera vaccines in reducing the incidence of cholera and associated mortality. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in October 2010 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT), and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The search aimed to identify both published and ongoing trials relevant to this topic. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that assessed oral cholera vaccines in healthy adults and children. Two independent authors evaluated the eligibility and risk of bias for each trial, and data extraction was performed by two independent reviewers. The data were analyzed using the Review Manager 5 software, with outcomes reported as vaccine protective efficacy (VE) along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The analysis incorporated data from seven large efficacy trials, four smaller artificial challenge studies, and 29 safety trials. Five different formulations of killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccines were evaluated in large-scale efficacy trials involving a total of 249,935 participants. The overall vaccine efficacy during the first year following vaccination was 52% (95% CI 35% to 65%), increasing to 62% (95% CI 51% to 62%) in the second year. However, the protective efficacy was notably lower in children under the age of five, at 38% (95% CI 20% to 53%), compared to 66% (95% CI 57% to 73%) in older children and adults. One trial conducted among military recruits during a small cholera epidemic demonstrated a protective efficacy of 86% (95% CI 37% to 97%) within four weeks of completing the two-dose vaccination schedule. However, efficacy data for currently available vaccine formulations beyond two years are lacking. Based on older trial data, it is unlikely that the protective effect of these vaccines extends beyond three years. Safety data for killed whole-cell vaccines did not reveal any clinically significant increase in adverse events compared to placebo. In contrast, only one live attenuated oral cholera vaccine has reached Phase III clinical trials, but it was found to be ineffective in a study involving 67,508 participants. Two new candidate live attenuated vaccines have shown promise in small artificial challenge studies, but they remain in the developmental stage. In conclusion, currently available oral killed whole-cell cholera vaccines provide 50% to 60% protection against cholera episodes during the first two years following the primary vaccination schedule. The decision to incorporate these vaccines into routine immunization programs in cholera-endemic regions will depend on factors such as the local prevalence of cholera, the frequency of outbreaks, and the availability of basic healthcare services, particularly those providing rapid rehydration therapy.
